extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers (especially those interested in narrative theory and craft)
extracted.subtask_description: A critical blog review evaluating Christopher Booker’s The Seven Basic Plots, focused on the book’s usefulness, methodology, style, and place in narrative scholarship. Intended to judge whether the work helps practitioners (writers, publishers, readers) or advances scholarly understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value / usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: “What possible value would this be? How could the knowledge be put to practical use?” — asks whether identifying basic plots actually helps publishers, booksellers, writers, or readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work produces actionable insights or practices for its intended stakeholders (publishers, booksellers, writers, readers). A taxonomy that cannot be applied in practical contexts scores poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on emotional effects vs plot taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The point is not that the number of plots is limited: it is that the number of possible emotional effects that can be created in the reader/audience is limited. The number of ways in which those emotions can be aroused, however, is infinite...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the book explains how narratives generate emotional effects (the craft) rather than merely listing abstract plot types; privileging insight into emotional mechanics is favoured over mere categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and concision / readability
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer objects to the book’s size: “It runs to 728 pages… I have a fundamental problem with non‑fiction books which are long… At one fifth the length, The Seven Basic Plots might be readable; as it is, it ain’t.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the content is appropriately condensed and edited for its purpose. Excessive length without clear necessity is a flaw; concision and readable pacing are positive attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor / systematic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of methodology: Has Booker been systematic? The reviewer quotes Booker: “I embarked… on an almost indiscriminate course of reading and re‑reading, through hundreds of stories of all kinds.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author uses a clear, reproducible method, explains selection criteria, and applies consistent analysis rather than impressionistic or indiscriminate sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical framework credibility (use of Freud/Jung)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer objects to reliance on Jung/Freud: “Booker has chosen to use Jung as a guide… Freud… is so hopelessly unscientific… when Jung is mentioned, I fear that the phrase ‘mumbo‑jumbo’ enters my head.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the intellectual credibility of the theoretical foundations: are they current, defensible, and appropriate to the claims? Reliance on discredited or shaky frameworks should be noted and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and proper attribution / bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about originality and sources: Booker mentions predecessors only in footnotes; NYT alleged he “lifted his ideas from ‘a wide spectrum of influential… writers and thinkers’.” The reviewer notes scant bibliography and dismissal of predecessors like Polti.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the work acknowledges prior scholarship, provides a thorough bibliography, and makes novel contributions rather than repackaging existing ideas without proper attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of purpose and audience (how‑to vs academic analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Booker doesn’t present us with a how‑to book for wannabe writers… This is a serious academic analysis.” The reviewer stresses knowing whether the book intends to instruct practitioners or analyze historically/theoretically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the author clearly states the book’s aims and intended audience, and whether the style, content, and organization align with that stated purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual clarity: definition of ‘plot’ vs archetype/situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and reviewer argue Booker confuses terms: “He’s not talking about ‘plot,’ you see, he’s talking about mythic structure or archetype… not plots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that key terms are defined precisely and consistently. Distinguish between plot (cause–effect sequences), archetype, motif, dramatic situation, and ensure the book does not conflate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of over‑generalisation / responsible readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer and NYT criticise “absurd generalisations about well known classics” and “inane readings of modern literature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether interpretations are supported by evidence and avoid sweeping, gratuitous claims about broad bodies of literature; encourage nuanced, defensible readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and editorial quality (facts, index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of factual errors and poor editorial work: “Poor old Booker occasionally gets even his facts wrong. He tells us that Peter Brook introduced Waiting for Godot… And now that I come to use it, the index isn’t reliable either.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify factual claims, dates, and attributions; ensure editorial elements (index, references, proofreading) meet professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal coherence / consistency across the book
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting a review: readers are advised to “peruse the informative first half and quickly ditch the second half of this 700‑plus page tome.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the book sustains quality and a coherent argument throughout, or whether different sections vary in value, leading to uneven usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability for practitioners (writers/screenwriters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer queries whether a writer would use the taxonomy: “Is he going to say, I shall write plot no.5 this time… so it’s sure to put me at the top of the bestseller list?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the book offers actionable, craft‑level guidance for writers and screenwriters or merely theoretical typologies; practical utility for creators is a distinct merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and accessibility (plain English vs academic gobbledygook)
rubrics_metrics.description: One positive: “The book is at least written in plain English, and not in academic gobbledygook.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge prose clarity and accessibility; plain language that communicates complex ideas effectively is a plus for broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning within scholarly tradition and engagement with predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: “This book belongs in a long tradition… There are few indications that Mr Booker realizes this – and certainly none in the bibliography.” Reviewer expects engagement with earlier work (Aristotle, Freytag, Polti, Campbell, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the book situates itself relative to prior scholarship and whether it engages, critiques, or builds upon earlier theorists appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market appeal and likely reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer and others speculate on sales and reception: hopes for popularity (reprints of Polti) and reports of mixed reviews across outlets (Sunday Telegraph, Daily Telegraph, Observer, Times, NYT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider likely reader/reviewer responses and commercial prospects; while not a sole quality measure, market reception can indicate whether the book resonates with intended audiences.
